title: A new positive
note: Fictional patients and staff. Confirmation testing, notifications, and screening decisions follow the physician, infection control, and current DOH and unit policy.
intro: You are the unit’s infection prevention nurse. On Tuesday the routine screening results arrive. Mr. Danilo Ocampo, 57, who dialyzes at station 10 on the Monday-Wednesday-Friday morning shift, has a positive hepatitis C antibody. His last result, six months ago, was negative. He was admitted to a hospital for pneumonia three months ago.

choices.text: Possible unit transmission: tell the physician, unit leaders, and infection control today.
choices.feedback: A new conversion is a cluster signal even as a single case: more than expected in a short time or place. The physician decides on confirmation; infection control and the clinical head decide what follows.

vitals.notified: Physician, head nurse, clinical head, IC (same day)

choices.text: Wait for next month’s screen to see if it is confirmed.
choices.feedback: A month lost is a month of possible further transmission and fading memory of what happened. Report the same day; confirmation runs alongside.
choices.then: You reconsider and notify everyone that afternoon.

vitals.notified: Physician, head nurse, clinical head, IC (same day)

choices.text: Tell the physician, who orders confirmation testing and will decide whether anyone else needs to know.
choices.feedback: The physician must know, but infection control and the unit leaders need to know the same day too. Notifying them is part of your role.
choices.then: You also tell the head nurse, the clinical head, and infection control.

vitals.notified: Physician, head nurse, clinical head, IC (same day)

choices.text: A line list and timeline: dates, stations, staff, vials, supplies, and outside exposures.
choices.feedback: Look for the common source: shared supplies, medication preparation, machines, a technique. His hospital stay is a possible source, but not a reason to skip the unit review.

vitals.list: Started: dates, stations, staff, vials, hospital stay

choices.text: Find out which nurse usually connects him and report her.
choices.feedback: Blame ends the investigation before it starts and teaches staff to hide problems. Look at systems and practices; a staff member’s technique is examined as part of the system, not as a verdict.
choices.then: You start a line list and timeline instead.

vitals.list: Started: dates, stations, staff, vials, hospital stay

choices.text: It probably came from his hospital stay three months ago; note that in the record and close the review.
choices.feedback: That may be true, but you cannot know without the review. Assuming an outside source is how unit transmission goes unnoticed.
choices.then: You start the line list and timeline.

vitals.list: Started: dates, stations, staff, vials, hospital stay

vitals.audit: Multi-dose vials drawn up at a cart beside stations 9–11

n3.scene: Watching the morning shift, you see heparin and other injectable medicines drawn up from multi-dose vials on a cart parked between stations 9 and 11, during connections.

choices.text: Audit all shifts, give feedback, ask why, and change the system.
choices.feedback: Medicines prepared near stations can be contaminated by blood on gloves and surfaces. The miss pattern usually points to a system problem; fix it and observe again.

vitals.audit: Checklist audits all shifts; prep area moved

choices.text: Send a memo reminding staff to be careful with vials.
choices.feedback: A memo changes little when the cart’s place in the room is the problem. Observe, ask why, and change the system.
choices.then: You observe across shifts and propose moving the preparation area.

vitals.audit: Checklist audits all shifts; prep area moved

choices.text: Observe the morning shift for a week with the checklist, since that is where the cart was seen.
choices.feedback: A start, but sample all shifts, including weekends; weekday audits can look far better than Saturdays.
choices.then: You extend observation to all shifts and propose moving the preparation area.

vitals.audit: Checklist audits all shifts; prep area moved

n4.scene: The head nurse asks you to leave Mr. Ocampo out of Friday’s quarterly report, “since it probably came from his hospital stay.”

choices.text: Count it by the definition and note the investigation.
choices.feedback: Never drop events to make a period look better. Surveillance only works when the same thing is counted the same way every time, even when the result is embarrassing.
A dropped event hides a possible transmission from the people who could stop the next one, and it breaks the series.
choices.then: You explain the rule and count it, with a note.

choices.text: Leave it out until the investigation is finished, then add it if the source turns out to be the unit.
choices.feedback: The definition decides whether it counts, not the investigation’s outcome. Count it now and note the investigation.

n5.scene: Patients at stations 9 and 11 ask you whether they “caught something too.”

choices.text: Say the team will speak with them; give the exposure list to infection control.
choices.feedback: Screening of exposed patients and public-health notification are decided by infection control and the unit’s leaders under current rules. Your list makes that decision possible. Mr. Ocampo’s result is his private information.

choices.text: Tell them Mr. Ocampo tested positive so they understand the risk.
choices.feedback: That discloses his private health information. The team communicates with each patient about their own risk.

choices.text: Reassure them there is nothing to worry about, since one positive result does not mean anyone else is affected.
choices.feedback: You do not know that yet. Say honestly that the team is reviewing and will talk with them.

end.title: Six weeks later
end.text: Mr. Ocampo’s infection was confirmed and he is in care. Additional screening of exposed patients found no other new cases. Medicines are now prepared in a clean area away from stations, and audits across all shifts show the change has held. The quarterly report shows the event, with the investigation and the system change noted.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • A new conversion is a cluster signal. Report the same day.
  • Investigate systems, not people: line list, timeline, shared supplies, medication preparation.
  • Observe across all shifts, ask why, change the system, remeasure.
  • Never drop an event from surveillance.
  • Screening and notification are decided by infection control and unit leaders; protect privacy.

See Observe a task, Make surveillance reproducible and Respond promptly.
